utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Malinic, I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic will now continue his cross-examination. Mr. Stojanovic you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you and good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I would like to ask you to tell the Trial Chamber in your estimate at what time did this reinforcement arrive that you requested from your Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lieutenant Benak with this part of the unit from the armoured transporter company came about an hour or two after our request for assistance, so that was probably around 9.00 a.m., and then an hour or an hour and a half after that, this part came from the 67th Communications Regiment and the section from the anti-aircraft division. So you could say that at 10.00 or 10.30 that last reinforcement part came to the field where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So at one point in time, were you able to draw out the unit and take the positions along the road, the Konjevic Polje-Kasaba road?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the reinforcements arrived, we worked on expanding the blockade line to deploy units along the road, so then this was completed when the unit came from the communications regiment. We linked up with the unit that was to the left of us, the police unit, perhaps at 10.00 and then when the units -- the unit from the communications regiment came, we just reinforced that particular sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And yesterday during the examination-in-chief, you mentioned that you also contacted the 5th Engineering Battalion and that you asked for equipment in order to be able to erect blockades at the place where these two units linked up. So could you tell us a little bit more about this?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if it was me who got in touch with the unit of the 5th Engineering Battalion, because they were not part of our force. It's most probable that I asked for this through the Chief of Staff, through the regiment, for them to get in touch, and to have an engineering unit come to me to block this part of the terrain which was not easily visible, and that was a problem. Also, night was coming so that would pose an additional problem. So that particular section of the terrain was blocked by engineering units of the Drina Corps. The reason for the request was that I didn't have the personnel or the equipment to do that myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you this so that you could tell me what do you mean when you say, "Block the positions." What was done?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The units of the Engineering Battalion took a part of the terrain that was not -- where the visibility was not good, and blocked it by placing different kinds of infantry mines in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: At which point in time did you receive information that you had your first prisoners?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had the first prisoners in the morning on the 13th of July, approximately at around 7.00 a.m. That was when the first three prisoners were brought to the barracks where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And can we now look at P1255 together, please? And I would just like to note again that it's under seal. This is the document that we looked at yesterday. Could we look at the next page in both versions of the document, please? And can we look at the next page in the English version as well, please? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And can we look at a part of this intercept together? Before we go into an analysis of that part of the conversation, I just want to ask you if you recall this conversation at all?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that it's possible that we talked, but I really couldn't say exactly what we talked about, and I couldn't really recognise that entirely in this particular intercept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, may I just jump in here? The question was different. Counsel asked you, "... I just want to ask you if you recall this conversation at all." Please answer this question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not entirely, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: But you recall that this conversation took part and that you were part of this conversation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I remember talking with different people on the 13th. I don't remember the content or the exact time. I don't remember if that was the person that I actually spoke to at 10.15, the person mentioned here. I can't really tell because that happened a long time ago, so I cannot really say yes, I remember that particular conversation on the 13th with this particular person. So that's why I'm saying it's possible that I did have the conversation but it's also possible that I did not have the conversation, if you get my meaning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, since the witness doesn't remember the conversation, we don't have to spend more time on it. The Chamber has the conversation by whomever in evidence and we'll have to interpret this evidence in the context of the totality of the evidence, so let's move on to another subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Then I'm going to put a similar question because I just wanted to ask this, actually put it in one sentence, but I'll do it this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, at any point in time did you have information that in the woods, in the direction in which the 28th Division column was moving, members of the column were killing each other?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And do you remember where you got this information from?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember the information because a couple of wounded people were brought out by members of the 28th Division, who were not wounded by infantry weapons. They had very serious wounds. I remember an example where one wounded person had his face completely blown off. Everything was open, the head, the skin. He was skill alive but this is something that will always stay with you. You remember it for the rest of your life. So this information came to me through these prisoners, those soldiers who brought that wounded person down to the medical station that was on the football pitch. So this is the information that I got about a part of the members of the 28th Division committing suicide and that there was in-fighting among them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And do you remember at all that you were asked that day on the 13th, at any point during the day -- or, you were told that along the road where you were, a delegation was supposed to pass comprising one Russian and one French person and that they were on their way to Bratunac, and this was along with the members of the column passing continuously?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at D301, please? D301. And can I please direct your attention at item 6. Your Honours, this is a statement of facts and plea agreement by the witness that we had the opportunity to hear a few days ago. In the statement of facts and during the examination-in-chief, among other things, in item 6, it says: "For most of the day of the 12th of July, I was in Potocari co-ordinating and working with Dusko Jevic, a commander of the MUP Special Police force, and following other military and MUP units." And then they are listed: Drina Corps military policemen, under Major Petrovic; members of the Drina wolves of the Zvornik Brigade; elements of the 10th Sabotage Detachment; elements of the 65th Protection Regiment military police, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What I want to ask you is this, Witness: Would this, in any way, change the position that you stated that on the 12th of July, you did not have any forces that you would be able to send to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: None of the members of the 65th Protection Regiment, except those who were engaged on the protection of General Mladic, was in Srebrenica or in Potocari. The only squad that was there at that point in time -- I didn't know where it was, probably with the commander of the Main Staff, but no other elements of the military police were engaged in Srebrenica or Potocari on the 12th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us, please, whether on the 13th of July at any point at your unit's command there was an UNPROFOR member?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: To the best of your recollection, when did you get in touch with them and how did this come about?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe these were -- this happened in the afternoon on the 13th of July when I was informed from the reception area, the lobby, that a member of the UNPROFOR wanted to see me. I received him at my office. We talked, and this member, and I believe he was a Dutch lieutenant, and a member of a unit that was stationed in Potocari explained to me that he had a problem, that some equipment had been seized, his equipment or their equipment, and that he would like to talk to someone who can assist in resolving this problem. He came to see us. We went to the battalion command, where one of my assistants made a list of all the equipment that had been confiscated, and we gave him a copy and another copy was kept on the premises of the battalion. And I promised that I would see what could be done about this with the help of the competent officers, in order to restore this equipment to the UN forces. There was a strict order that no equipment should be confiscated from UNPROFOR members, UN members, that they should not be taken prisoner and that they should be assisted as much as possible on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will now put another question. Can you tell us, to the best of your recollection, whether there was any mention about where this equipment had been confiscated, in what area?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that this was noted in the -- on the list and the document that was prepared on this occasion. I can't tell you exactly where this happened. I believe there was mention of the area but I can't really recall as I sit here, and I can't recall who it was who had done that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us, if you recall, whether there was any mention about the identity of these persons who confiscated the equipment?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't really say. As I sit here, I don't know whether there were members of the Army of Republika Srpska or police members or civilians, for that matter. I can't really say for certain. But it's probably -- it was probably noted down and this lieutenant, he took a copy of the document, the list, whereas the copy that we had, that we kept, was forwarded to the regiment archives. So I can't really tell you with certainty anything about it at this point, as I sit here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us, please, what happened after that, once you took this down and made this note or logged this in the logbook?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The lieutenant requested that I escort him with my men to Potocari, but I couldn't do that because of the situation that I was in, and the lieutenant, who was in touch with his command, he decided to stay at the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: To the best of your recollection, how long did they stay there in the barracks?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two to three days, as far as I can remember, they stayed at the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: During those two or three days were they free to move around, as far as you were concerned?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: UN members had the full freedom of movement. They had their weapons on them and the entire equipment that they had come with. They were armed, in other words, and they were provided a room where they could sleep and be on their own. They had their vehicles with them, and communications equipment. And I believe that at one point the lieutenant said that he was on line with his base in Split and I assumed that he was also linked -- had communications with the Potocari battalion, with his battalion in Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned three prisoners in early morning on the 13th of July, and that they were kept at the -- at your unit command's facilities. What was happening?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, these weren't really facilities of any sort. This was just a house, a private home, that was next to a -- the school building, and there was a garage or that sort of thing, like a shed, and in addition to these three, the -- some ten other prisoners were brought there. Those were the first -- the first batch that was coming in. But as the number of prisoners grew, we organised their accommodation at the stadium. The prisoners who were held in that building, or rather in that house, were transferred to the stadium during the day, and when they joined the other prisoners who had been taken prisoner on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: At some point in time, did you receive any information to the effect that a TV crew might come to film these prisoners at the stadium, at the football pitch?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received an order, not information. I believe this order came from Lieutenant-Colonel Jazic, where he said that TV crews would come to my sector and that they should be assisted in filming all of this, that it should be facilitated for them, that they shouldn't be checked, that there was no need to screen them but just to make it possible for them to do their job. This would have been sometime around noon, I believe. That's my assumption. I think it was about noon time on the 13th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you enable them to do this? Did you make it possible?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The crews did arrive. I think there were at least three crews including a foreign crew, and they had the full freedom to film all the developments on the football pitch in Nova Kasaba.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: At any point in time, did you take any steps in order to provide medical assistance to the prisoners who were held there at the football pitch?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That morning, when these activities began, when we realised the situation we were in, and when combat operations began as part of this, through the president of the municipality of Milici, we employed a medical team from the Milici hospital who came -- who went to the stadium to provide medical care, not just to the prisoners but also to members of my unit who had been wounded. So there were no exceptions or no special treatment of one's or the other's. This medical team remained there the whole day.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the last portion of the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the last portion of your answer. What we have on the record is, "This medical team remained there the whole day." What did you say after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Until the prisoners left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember whether there were any logistical facilities in order to provide water to these people at the pitch?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Some of the equipment that we took from the municipality, but also the bags, the military satchels that we had, the water we had there, we engaged people to get water for the prisoners, and the president of the municipality was also very helpful in this. He helped us get some food for the prisoners, primarily bread, because the Milici bakery also produced bread for the barracks -- for the men in the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: At any point in time, did you receive information to the effect that there was some construction work going on near the football pitch, that there was some digging going on and heavy equipment used for that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please pull in e-court 04179, a 65 ter document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: This document, sir, is something that you were asked about in the previous trial where you testified at length, and I will just have a few questions. Do you remember -- can you remember, have you ever seen this document, and when, if so?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I saw this document for the first time in 2005.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Is this a document that was shown to you by the investigators on the 14th of December, 2005, when they interviewed you, the ICTY investigators?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: After that first perusal of this document, I would like to ask you, can you tell us, as you sit here, whether you call whether at any point in time on that day on the 13th of July --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the last portion of the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, could you repeat the last portion of your question which was not caught by the interpreters?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So my question was whether after the elapsed time, after so much time has elapsed, can you tell us, as you sit here, whether you can recall whether you had received this document on that day, on the 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't have any recollection of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In military terms, in the signals system that you had in place, the system of communications, would such a document in this format, would it be possible for it to reach your unit? Could you get a document of this format?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you mean a telegram format or if your reference is to the format of an order, the answer is no. But if your question is whether it could have reached me in any other way, my answer would be yes, there would be such a possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The reason I ask this is because we see in the heading of this document, on line 3, where it says that it should be forwarded to the commander of the Military Police Battalion of the 65th Motorised Protection Regiment, and then the word "order" follows. So I ask you: At any point in time, did you or did you not receive -- whether you received an order of this type or not, would you have taken action pursuant to it? Would you have obeyed it or acted upon it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Had I received such an order, I would have acted on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Then my next question is: At any point in time, to the best of your recollection, did you prohibit any filming or taking photographs of the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I had an order where it said that the teams would arrive and that they were entitled, allowed, to film everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you explain whether this was a written order or whether it was an oral order; and if it was an oral order, by whom it was given?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you mean the order about the arrival of the TV crews?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You said -- the one you just referred to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that I already answered that question but I will repeat that. Lieutenant-Colonel Jazic called to say that the -- that TV crews would come to the Kasaba stadium and that they had the right to film. I don't think that Lieutenant-Colonel Jazic issued the order on his own. He probably wasn't authorised to do so, but that was probably an order from the superior command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Why would he not be authorised to do so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because it wasn't in his remit to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Why was it probably an order from the superior command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, because the Main Staff also had a press center, and part of their duties was film documentation, so they were probably the ones who organised the filming. They would take the TV crews out in the field throughout the whole republic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I put a follow-up question to that. Witness, earlier you said that three film teams arrived that the location, at the football pitch, one was a foreign one. Can you tell us from which country?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot really say, perhaps it was British. The people in the press centre would know that better. I didn't really pay attention to that. I didn't do any checks, because it was said that they didn't need to be vetted. It was not my -- part of my duties to deal with reporters or TV crews. I had some other duties that I was paying attention to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: How many people were part of these three TV teams?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said, as far as I can remember, it was at least three, and there were at least 10 or 12 people there in those TV crews that appeared in the field, in the area, on the 13th of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Ten people altogether or every team comprised by ten people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. It wasn't each crew. It was a total of 10 to 12 people in all the crews together. I don't know how many people there were in each crew.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: How did you establish that these people were three teams, three crews, and not one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were three or more, as I said, because there were several cameras, so I got the impression that it was several crews. They also had the logos on the cameras. I wasn't really paying attention to who was coming. Once I received the order, then it's quite a natural, normal thing that you would let them do their job.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for the help.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 2, it says here: "Prohibit traffic for all United Nations vehicles on route Zvornik-Vlasenica. Until further notice, re-route them via Zvornik-Sekovici-Vlasenica and back." I'm asking you at any point in time on that day, the 13th of July, or later, did you stop or prevent the passage of UN vehicles along the road where your unit was deployed?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And then in item 4, it states, "The commander of the military police battalion --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We do not see the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: "... will get in touch with General Miletic and receive from him additional orders and verify if the proposal has been approved. And verify if the proposal has been approved by the commander of the VRS Main Staff." I'm asking you now: Do you recall, on this basis, if you got in touch with General Miletic and asked him whether all of this that was written by the commander of the Main Staff was also approved?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Had I received the document, I would have probably acted pursuant to the order and asked General Miletic about these activities, but as I said, I don't remember. I don't recall seeing the order. So probably I did not get in touch with General Miletic on this particular issue in order to resolve it. It's a little bit illogical, the sense of it, because it's an order but then I'm also supposed to contact somebody to verify if the order was actually issued. So it's a little bit illogical. Probably the first step is to co-ordinate the steps that need to be taken and then send a specific order to me as the commander of the unit as to what to do and what measures to take.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning to you, Your Honours and everyone. I don't mean to be problematic, but in the question that Mr. Stojanovic put to the witness, there appears at page 15, lines 23 through 25, the question was: "... on this basis, if you got in touch with General Miletic and asked him whether all of this that was written by the commander of the Main Staff was also approved?" There is no indication in the document that this was written by the commander of the Main Staff, so I'm not sure that the question is -- that the answer is responsive to the question or the question was framed as Mr. Stojanovic had intended to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, what made you suggest in the question that it was an order issued by the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, you will see from the documents that follow. But I would just like us to focus once again on item 4, item 4 of the document which I literally read, in which the commander of the military police battalion is asked to get in touch with General Miletic and receive from him additional orders and verify if the proposal, this proposal, has also been approved by the commander of the VRS Main Staff. That's what I read in Article 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think I would like to help with this. There is perhaps a misunderstanding or it's the way it was put to the witness. I understand the question to be: If you got in touch with General Miletic and asked him whether all of this that was written was also approved by the commander of the Main Staff. That is, I think, the gist of the question. And I'm of the view that the witness answered that question, if this was really what was asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I misinterpreted it, my apologies. I always appreciate the assistance of my colleagues. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Yes, that is precisely what the question was. Now can we look at document 04026? And, Judge Fluegge, thank you very much. We know to that this document has been looked at many times. 04026, this is a 65 ter document. That's the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And I would like to ask you to look at it. This is a document by the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska of the 13th of July, 1995. Before we go back to the first page again, Your Honours, could we please zoom in on and look at the stamp on this document? And we would be able to see on the right-hand side of the stamp the time. I see that it says here, if I'm not mistaken, Witness, in the part that says "approved," the time, I think 2235 hours and then in the section "approved" it's 2239 on the 13th of July, 1995. I would now like to ask you this, with a request to look at the heading of the document in the B/C/S and we already see it in the English, this document, among other things or other places, was also sent to, we are looking at "to," the 65th Motorised Protection Regiment. Did you in the field at any point in time have the opportunity to acquaint yourself with this document?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if it's not a problem, may I just have a little bit of time to look at the document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Looking at the document, we see in the English translation only that there was a delivery stamp but no further details. Is there any way, because there is far more information, it seems, in that stamp, perhaps parts illegible, but that we can have access to that as well? Mr. Vanderpuye, do you agree that the English version only --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: There is a second page in the English version which should reflect the information contained in the stamp. So if we go to page 2 in the English we should see the information that's contained in the stamp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's of course where I looked, Mr. Vanderpuye. Of course, if it's at the bottom of the document I look at the bottom of the English document as well, that it says, "stamp," that there's two stamps at the bottom of this document, one is a command stamp and the other is a delivery stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I have in e-court, I have just delivery stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you ask -- before you give me guidance to go to page 2, I'd say go to page 2 first yourself, because I had done that already.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, I wasn't intending to give you guidance. I only saw page 1 on e-court, and that's what I assumed that the Chamber was referring to. So I didn't know you had already moved to page 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course I would do that. I would not ask questions about stamps at the bottom without looking at the bottom of the English version as well. Therefore, I said the delivery stamp is only there by saying delivery stamp without any further details. I would not have said that unless I would have verified that in e-court which I did. Is there any way to get a fuller translation of that portion of the document where it says, "delivery stamp"?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, I can look into that and maybe there is another version of it. I'll look for it just now and I'll -- I'll let the Chamber know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Otherwise, I think it would be advisable that the parties sit together and see to what extent they can read that stamp, because some words are -- well, at least readable, legible. Other parts may be more problematic in that respect. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, just one question: Did you ever have the opportunity to see this document?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's possible that I saw it in 2005 during my interview at The Hague Tribunal offices in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And during the war, on the night between the 13th and the 14th or the 14th and the 15th of July, did you have the opportunity to look at the document?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can see that it was sent to the command of the 65th Motorised Protection Regiment. It was at the command which happened to be located in Crna Rijeka. I don't think that the regiment command would send out an original source order like this one. If they received the order then probably on the basis of this order they would draft their own order with similar items for those parts that referred to my unit and the section in which I was in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The question was: Did you have the opportunity to look at the document during the war? Please answer that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that in this form and in this format, probably not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Did you see it in a different format?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't know if you understand me. The dispatch, the telegram, is addressed to the protection regiment. If the command of the protection regiment received this telegram --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sir, I have to stop you. It is a simple question, you can say yes or no, did you see that at the relevant point in time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you -- and I'm going to finish with this document with this question: Did you at any point in time act upon the instructions in this order referred to in the text that you have in front of you, on the 14th, the 15th or onwards?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A lot of the things here do not concern my unit, sections, and axes and places and settlements are referred to that were not in my area of responsibility at the time. Perhaps the only relevant part would be not to permit the arrival of journalists in the sector of combat. That's the only thing, as well as to prevent the passage of UNPROFOR forces, but I couldn't do that. They could have done that somewhere else. I was in the middle. They could have been dealing with that part outside of that. I already had UN forces at my barracks. So that I practically did not act pursuant to this order. I did not drive the members of the UN forces out of my barracks, had I received any orders to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And -- thank you. In view of your experience up to that part, would it have been natural during combat to expect the -- all people who had no business there or all uninvited people to prevent them from coming to that combat area?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is a general rule, not only in the Yugoslav People's Army and the Army of Republika Srpska which took over all those rules, but these are rules of combat that apply in all armies in the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I just try to understand? You earlier told us that you gladly accepted the presence of television crews, three in numbers, and that you had not received that order, and that you told us that, of course, the freedom of movement of UN was the most normal and logical thing to do. Now, looking at this order, you say, of course it would be illogical to allow anyone to be there, whereas a minute ago, when you apparently -- you had not received this order, you considered it, may I assume, logical, to do just the opposite? So I have some difficulties in reconciling your logic as developed by your own behaviour and the logic as we find it now in this document. Do you have an explanation for that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I did not have the authority to take decisions on whether TV crews would be -- would come to my sector or not. That is something that was the purview of the superior command or the command of the Main Staff. In this particular situation, it wasn't me who was to decide or who was even consulted whether I should allow the teams to come in and film or not. There was an order informing me that these TV crews would come to film this, and to film the developments at the pitch and in Kasaba. Now, as for me, the activity of TV crews and journalists in combat areas, I believe, are unacceptable for the reason of security of those crews or journalists. And in my view they should not be allowed to access such areas, but I did have an order and I acted on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will now deal with the arrival of General Mladic, but I see the time and perhaps we could go on break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We will take a break, and we will first move into closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Stojanovic, perhaps it would be best if you restart your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, at one point in time, on the 13th of July, you were informed that General Mladic was coming. Where were you when that information arrived?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received information that General Mladic had arrived outside -- I was not at the stadium. I don't know whether I was on the front line or in the barracks, I can't really recall, but I received the information via a Motorola unit, that's the equipment we use, so basically I received information that the commander of the Main Staff, General Mladic, had arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any information that General Mladic would come previously?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There were no indications or prior announcements that General Mladic would visit Nova Kasaba.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us, to the best of your ability, at about what time General Mladic made an appearance at the football pitch in Nova Kasaba?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, that was in the afternoon, perhaps between 5.00 and 6.00 p.m. or thereabouts. That was when General Mladic arrived at the football pitch in Nova Kasaba.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we take a look together at a document, P1132? And if we could have page 43 in e-court? Your Honours, this is the photo album compiled by Jean-Rene Ruez, and we need the photo on page 43.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognise this area and this field?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In this aerial photo, we see that this was taken at around 2.00 p.m. Now, the first thing I would like to ask you is whether you can remember that at about this time the prisoners were grouped in these two different groups, as we can see in the photo?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, whether this second group is a group of prisoners, that is something that remained unclear the last time I testified. It is possible that these are prisoners, but it's also possible that these were people from Milici and the surrounding areas who were there at the stadium. So I still have doubts about what this is. There was a group of prisoners who were waiting to be registered, lists were supposed to be compiled of prisoners, and there were officers at the field who were compiling these lists. So I can't really say with any certainty either way.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If you thought these were people from Milici, what would they have been doing on the ground there and just sitting there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Well, some people from Milici were present there at the stadium, although this was probably my mistake, a mistake on my part. I shouldn't have allowed it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What would they have been doing there at the stadium? What was the purpose of their gathering there on the pitch?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The purpose of their being there on the pitch was to identify the prisoners because some of these men were people they knew very well and had worked with up until recently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And who had asked them to identify the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No one asked for that. It was their own will. They even were given the opportunity to talk to these neighbours of yore if they recognised any one amongst the group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I have one follow-up question in that respect. Did they then spontaneously gather at this football pitch in the middle of this war turmoil? Is that how I have to understand your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This was a spontaneous gathering of the people from Milici and the surrounding areas. They had heard, they had been informed, that a large number of members of the division were kept prisoner at the stadium and perhaps it was a mistake on my part to allow anyone to be there, but that was the situation then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you specifically allowed them in there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, for all practical purposes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You were not ordered to do so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, you explained to us before the break that it was far too dangerous for anyone who had nothing to do there, television crews, or -- to be around because that was only logical, as you explained to us, that people should stay out. And nevertheless, I allowed possibly this second group to be lined up that nicely in this football pitch and spontaneously coming there and being allowed by you to identify the prisoners? Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. And I've said that I probably made a mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mistake of what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, a mistake. It was a mistake to allow unauthorised personnel to be there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I was mainly interested whether this was your testimony. You have confirmed that. Mr. Stojanovic you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I have a follow-up again. Now, you say you allowed these people to come in. At page 26, lines 6 to 14 - I'm not going to read all that - you say: "It is possible that these are prisoners, but it's also possible that these were people from Milici." Are you now changing from that position and saying you know definitely that these were people from Milici? Is that now your position? Because you allowed them? It's not a possibility now, it's a definite fact? Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I've said I'm not sure. It is possible that these people who had come from Milici, that they were under these trees so you can't really see them. That is a possibility because I know that there was a number of civilians there without weapons at the stadium. Now, whether they were there precisely at this time or not, I can't really say with certainty but I do know that some civilians were present at the stadium.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We then understand your testimony to be that you saw people, you didn't know who they were, you just thinking that they are possibly from Milici, and without knowing their identity you allowed them to be there to identify the prisoners? Is that how we must understand you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I said that I wasn't sure whether this group --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not asking you what you said. I said is that how we must understand your testimony, that you allowed people whose identity you're not even sure of who they are, they could jolly well be enemy and you just bring them there to identify prisoners because you're saying it is possible? You're not saying definitely these are people from Milici.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A number of civilians who had come and who were at the stadium, I knew these people, and next to them there were people --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm stopping you. Please answer my question, and if you don't want to answer, say you don't want to answer my question. Is that how we must understand your testimony, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I cannot answer with a yes or no. I can say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Im asking you to answer with a yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you're putting me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I stop you there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- in a tight spot here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I stop you. I stop you there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't really answer with a yes or no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic should wait -- Mr. Mladic should stop for a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I stop you there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic should wait for a second to consult with counsel and should keep his voice at a low volume.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you should wait for a second. We will just continue meanwhile.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sir, is that how we must understand your testimony, yes or no? That's what I'm asking you. Don't tell me I'm putting you in a spot.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Some people who were sitting there I knew but not all of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm stopping you. Do you want to answer my question or not? I'm asking you a different question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot answer your question with a yes or no. It's impossible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I have also a follow-up question on this matter. I would like to take you back to the beginning of this line of questioning. This aerial photograph was shown to you and you were asked -- the first question was: "... whether you can remember that at about this time, the prisoners were ground in these two different groups, as we can see them on the photograph?" You started your answer by saying: "Now, whether this second group is a group of prisoners, that is something that remained unclear the last time I testified. It is possible that these are prisoners but it is also possible that these were people from Milici and surrounding areas ..." So the whole line of questioning started clearly with two groups of prisoners where you said, Well, whether the second group are prisoners or are people from Milici, I'm not sure about that. After a few follow-up questions, you suddenly positioned the Milici people invisible under trees. Therefore, you're just deviating from previous answers and you're deviating from the question. Do you have any explanation about why suddenly you are -- why you suggested that the second group visible on the photograph may have been people from Milici, why you suddenly changed that and make them invisible people from Milici under the trees? Do you have an explanation for that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as I've already said, there are two possibilities. At this point, I can't really say what the situation was at 2.00 p.m. on the 13th of July. I told you what the -- about the second group, there were two possibilities: One is that these are prisoners who are waiting their turn to be registered, and the other possibility is that these were people from Milici, civilians, who were there who had come to view the prisoners. So I am not disputing at all this second group in the field. Now, in this other possibility, that these are prisoners who are waiting to be registered, that included the possibility that the civilians were under the trees on the sidelines. As I sit here and after all this time that has elapsed, I can't really confirm and say with certainty which is which.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Fluegge has one or more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed. Mr. Malinic, how many people from Milici were present there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't really say the number. I can't recall. Maybe 50 or 30. I can't really say. I didn't count them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: How did you establish that they were from Milici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because most of the people there, I knew. And I socialised with them in Milici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Were they Serbs or Muslims, or both?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the time, as far as I know, there were only Serbs in Milici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I'm not asking about the people in Milici. In this group which you indicated that they were probably from Milici, if they were Serbs or Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: How could they be able to identify the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if you're standing 20 or 30 metres away and you see a man that you had worked with until very recently, then you may know his name, first and last name. You can recognise that person, if I can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Did anybody call these people from Milici to come there for identification purposes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Their role was not to identify these people on behalf of the military organs. It was like a personal act to recognise their co-workers or colleagues that they had worked with until just earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Did you compile a list of those people from Milici so that you can follow up if there was perhaps a mistake or a misidentification?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Were these people from Milici civilians? Or were they in uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that they were all civilians. I don't know if they were militarily engaged or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: What about uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think so, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Were women among this group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is a considerable possibility of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please describe the identification process. How was that carried out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I said, it was not an organised identification process. It was an act of every person who wanted to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please describe how that was carried out, not in general terms, but what could a person who was standing there, and you were there, could see how that was carried out? Describe that, please, so that I have a picture and can understand what you are talking about.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot describe it precisely, but I can tell you in principle, if you come and look at the prisoners and you see and recognise somebody with whom you worked or who was your neighbour, then those civilians could talk with those prisoners, they could go up to them and speak with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: How can they speak to each other if they are grouped in that way as we see it on the aerial photograph on the screen? How can they speak to each other individually?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because the person who was recognised by the person who had come from Milici would not stay in that group. They would stand up and stand next to the group and talk. But I cannot confirm to you how many such examples there were or give you the exact number. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Why were these people -- if the left group on the screen on this picture was the group of the people from Milici, why were they grouped in such a strict order? Who gave this order to be grouped in that way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No one lined up those civilians who arrived and followed what was going on in the stadium. That's why I said that one of the possibilities is that these were not civilians, this other circled group, but that these are members of the 28th Division who were waiting for their names to be taken down. At that point in time, I was unsure as to the disposition on the stadium and the things that were happening on the 13th of July at the stadium. I gave you two options, and I explained each one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I heard that, yes, thank you. Since we are dealing with this situation there on the football pitch, I have an additional question about the lists of prisoners which were compiled. How many members of your unit were present during this registration process?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was one superior officer, he was a general affairs desk officer, so his role in the battalion was just general information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I asked you about the number. How many members of your unit were present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Three or four soldiers at the most, and the senior officer were given the task of taking down the names and making the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Only the senior officer was given this task, to make -- to prepare the list; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was a -- not a senior officer but it was a general affairs desk officer in the battalion. He was a sergeant first class in the battalion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This was not my question. I asked you that only this person was tasked to prepare the list; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: How many names did he put on the list during this process until it was stopped?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said he was the only superior officer. Some people were helping him. I don't know the number of people who were helping.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I asked you if this person was the only one who compiled the list. Now you are saying other people helped him. And you don't know the number. You were in charge of this group. Can you tell me how many names were put on the list and how many pages were -- how many pages were used for this purpose?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know how to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would just direct Your Honour's attention to page 35, line 4, when the witness immediately said: "Three or four soldiers at the most, and the senior officer were given the task ..." So that's maybe what creates the confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is possible. Thank you very much for that intervention. Have you ever seen the list?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Did you have -- had you had the opportunity to hold them in your own hands?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yesterday already we talked about the purpose of this registration process. And then you told us it was not used any more, it was then later given to a certain officer and then put in the archives. Why was that list compiled and why wasn't it used for preparation of the exchange you testified about yesterday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The main thing when you capture somebody is to take down their particulars. This is the main thing according to the rules of the military police. And that was the main reason to take down the names of the detainees, the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please, not again what you already said. I would like to know why was it not used for that purpose, for the exchange of prisoners? Why was it not used for that purpose?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I was not in charge of the prisoner exchange. Why didn't anyone ask for the list? And it is known that the list was made. This is the question that goes beyond what I know, beyond my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you, no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have one follow-up question. How far is the distance between Milici and the football pitch in Nova Kasaba?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Two to 2 and a half kilometres or 2 and a half to 3 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How did these people from Milici arrive? Did they come by car or?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really couldn't say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us, to your best recollection, how long General Mladic stayed among those people?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Mladic, if I remember correctly, stayed up to 30 minutes at the Nova Kasaba stadium, up to 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And did he come from the direction of Konjevic Polje?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which direction General Mladic came from. He was already there when I arrived, so I wasn't at the stadium when he arrived in order to be able to say from which direction he had come.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And did you see the vehicle that General Mladic arrived in?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, yes. I think it was parked next to the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us what type of vehicle it was?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot really specify the type of vehicle. I think it was a Puh.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And were there any other vehicles escorting General Mladic's vehicle, armoured personnel carriers or any other kind of vehicle?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think not. There were no armoured personnel carriers. As for whether there were any other vehicles in the escort of General Mladic's vehicle, I really cannot say because I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Where was General Mladic standing while he addressed the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Mladic walked among them. If we look at this photograph and this image, he walked among the prisoners. He wasn't standing in front of them. He walked among them. I don't know whether he went in 3, 4 or 5 metres deep but he was among them in this area that is marked with a rectangle.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: How far were you at that point from the place where General Mladic was?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I arrived, I stood practically at the forward edge. I didn't walk among the prisoners. I was standing at the line where the prisoners were.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You heard what General Mladic told the prisoners; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A part of it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell the Trial Chamber what you heard? What did General Mladic say to the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not able to interpret exactly General Mladic's words. I can just tell you generally what topics he talked about. They were war, Alija Izetbegovic. As I said, it's what I remember. People become casualties on the basis of unthought-out decisions, and that is why the prisoners do not need to be afraid because they would return to their houses and be exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And do you remember if any of the prisoners addressed General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember if -- I don't remember that anybody actually stood up and said anything. But there is a possibility that people were saying things out loud, that they were giving confirmation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, would you please stop the witness when he expresses the word "there is a possibility." We have heard so many possibilities. Thinking of possibilities, everyone can do that. We would like to hear his testimony about what he observed, what he heard, what he saw, not about what he thinks could be a possibility. Unless he has any --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- facts, he can present the facts he observed and then whether there are any possibilities, if that is an obvious start of such a line of questioning, then you can ask him about it. But as soon as this witness spontaneously comes up with possibilities, you're invited to stop him, and otherwise the Chamber will do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before you carry on, I have a clarification question. Sir, what -- did Mr. Mladic address these people as he was walking amongst them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Mladic didn't walk among them. He stepped among them and then he was standing in one spot. And that's where he spoke to them. He addressed them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I just want to refer to your testimony a few minutes ago when you said he was walking amongst them, which is what triggered my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think that I said that he walked among them. I said that he stood among them, "usao medju njim." He walked into this place marked with a rectangle. I think this is what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We have in the transcript page 39, line 11, the sentence, "General Mladic walked among them."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And if you say that there is a transcription or a translation error we will be glad to verify it. Then we listen to our own language and then it will be verified whether it's transcribed properly and whether it's translated properly. If you insist on that, no problem, we'll do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you insist on it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. That should be repeated, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, then I should read the full answer you gave, and you should consider if that is really your request. Lines 11 to 15, the record shows: "General Mladic walked among them. If we look at this photograph and this image, he walked among the prisoners. He wasn't standing in front of them. He walked among them. I don't know whether he went in 3, 4 or 5 metres deep but he was among them in this area that is marked with this rectangle." Four times you said that he walked among them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you still insist on that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honours, this could be a nuance of interpretation. "Stood among them," "stepped among them" is a possibility as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My question then still stands, was he among them as he spoke to them? He wasn't standing outside the group and facing them and addressing them, that's my question. He talked to them while he was among them. Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, can you please tell us if you recall what the reaction of the prisoners was after General Mladic addressed them?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Mladic, once he stopped talking, he was applauded by the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: After this visit to the stadium, did you see where General Mladic was headed?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Mladic left towards Milici.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember whether General Mladic at any point went to the facilities that you referred to as the facilities of your command?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: How far is it, in terms of time, to get from the football pitch in Kasaba to Vlasenica, driving at a normal speed?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The same question: How long would it take you to get from the crossing in Konjevic Polje to the Kasaba football pitch?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ten minutes at most.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On those days, did you have occasion in any other situation to run into General Mladic or to meet him?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We will briefly go through this document and then I will conclude. But tell me, at this point in time, did you have any tasks that had to do with searching the terrain?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 16th or 17th of July, Lieutenant-Colonel Keserovic, I believe, came and said that the terrain would be swept and that -- referring to the area between Srebrenica towards the communication to Milici and Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Who was supposed to take part in this sweeping of the terrain?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, the terrain sweep was supposed to be carried out by the Bratunac Brigade, whereas my task, or my unit's task, was to remain where we had been since the morning of 13th of July and to remain there blocking that area through the end of the terrain search.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Who issued this task to you, specifically?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That my unit will be tasked with blocking the area during the search of the terrain, this was issued to us, this task, by Lieutenant-Colonel Keserovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, whether it is your understanding that when you get such a task, a task of searching the terrain after combat, is this a legal military activity?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether you were involved in this for more than a day?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did your unit, during the execution of this task, have any imprisoned members of the 28th Division, any prisoners?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether some other units that participated in the search of the terrain captured any prisoners as a result of this search of terrain?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I first learned that there were some people taken prisoner during the search. I first learned this information during the Tolimir trial when I testified. I learned it from the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know that police units also took part in searching the terrain, civilian police?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I expressed my doubts about this entire activity of searching the terrain because the unit doing this has to link up with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are not interested to hear the doubts of the witness. He can tell us whatever fact he knows, he observed, or he heard. And then whether that creates doubt or not is -- so, please, would you rephrase your question, Mr. Stojanovic? Well, even there, do you have any fact to your knowledge which would indicate that the police units also took part in searching the terrain, that is civilian police? Do you have any fact to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My left neighbour were Zvornik police units, and if we talk about units that took part, they were in a blockade, and this was part of the activities involving the search of the terrain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No ifs and ands, please. Your left neighbours were Zvornik police units, okay, that's fine. What now -- if we talk about -- no ifs -- any fact you know about your left neighbour Zvornik police units which is relevant, please tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, when you interrupted me a little earlier, all those were facts. I -- it was not my intention to talk about possibilities or probability. When I say facts --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. -- please answer my question, if you're able to do so; if not, the next question will be put to you by Mr. Stojanovic. You talked about that your left neighbours were Zvornik police units. Anything to add to that fact which may be relevant for this Chamber to finally know whether police units took part in searching the terrain, that is civilian police units, any fact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the combat operation of terrain search consists of units that are in blockade. They take up positions along a certain line and then there is -- there are elements of units that search, that comb the terrain. Now, the police unit participated in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, next question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I believe that the sentence was left hanging but I will continue, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, in those days, at any point in time, did you see or hear that the prisoners of war who were in the area of responsibility of your battalion had been -- that any war crimes had been committed against them?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have any information about what happened to the prisoners who left the stadium in Nova Kasaba, so, in that sense, I had no information as to what was done with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And my final question: Did you ever, while you were in that area in July 1995, see any work done involving the sanitation of the area, the restoring, restoration of the field, "asanacija," the collection of the bodies and so on?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A part of that work was done by the civilian bodies of the Milici municipality, so a part of the terrain was restored by civilians of the Milici municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Stop you again. What -- and that was the question, what did you see in this respect? Did you see any work done involving the sanitation of the terrain? Did you see something or did you not see something? And then we'll have some follow-up questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that a part of the terrain --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Stop. No. What you know -- the question what is you saw. Could you please tell us whether you saw anything as far as the sanitation of the terrain is concerned. That's a simple yes or no, I take it. Either you did see something or you did not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't see anything. No, I didn't see anything. But I did have knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no. The question has been answered. The witness did not see anything. Please, next question, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: My next question: What did you know about the sanitation of the terrain, and did you have any knowledge that had to do with the areas where the bodies were buried?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about the sites where the bodies were buried, but I know that the civilian authorities of the Milici municipality took steps to restore the terrain to carry out the sanitation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: A short question, again, in relation to the football pitch. You told us that there was the group of the civilians from Milici. Were they still present when Mr. Mladic arrived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not sure that they were there when General Mladic arrived.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: When did they leave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot say with any precision when it was that they left that area, the area of the football field.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: How did they leave and go back to Milici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that they left individually, just the way they had come. Now, whether they -- whether they used any vehicles or whether they had walked there, I really don't know. I can't tell you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I have a problem now with your testimony, sir. You told us earlier that you called these people to identify, isn't it so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no. That's not how it is. I never said that I had called these people to identify someone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
